review_items.mechanism_name: De novo mevalonate/cholesterol biosynthesis pathway enzymes in hepatocytes
review_items.mechanism_summary: Program P21 encodes nearly the complete enzymatic cascade for de novo sterol biosynthesis via the mevalonate pathway in mouse hepatocytes. Early steps: Hmgcs1 (acetoacetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA), Idi1 (IPP/DMAPP isomerase), Fdps (farnesyl-PP synthase), Mvk/Pmvk/Mvd (mevalonate kinase cascade converting mevalonate to isopentenyl-PP). Squalene synthesis: Fdft1 (squalene synthase, first committed step to sterols). Post-squalene: Lss (lanosterol synthase), Cyp51 (lanosterol 14α-demethylase), Tm7sf2 (sterol C14-reductase), Msmo1/Erg28/Nsdhl (C4-demethylation complex, where ERG28 is the non-catalytic scaffold), Hsd17b7 (zymosterone reductase), Sc5d (lathosterol C5-desaturase), Dhcr7 (7-DHC reductase, last step to cholesterol). Acat2 esterifies the resulting cholesterol. Hepatocyte-specific knockout of Cyp51 causes liver injury (oval cell response, fibrosis); TM7SF2 deficiency causes lipid accumulation and ER stress in regenerating liver. Hepatic expression of NSDHL, HSD17B7, and MSMO1 is well established. The complete pathway is explicitly catalogued in comprehensive reviews of cholesterol biosynthesis.

assessor_text.text: Mevalonate pathway deregulation has been observed in several diseases, including Mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD). MKD is a hereditary auto-inflammatory disorder, due to mutations at mevalonate kinase gene (MVK), encoding mevalonate kinase (MK) enzyme. MVK mutations have been reported as associated with impairment of mevalonate pathway with consequent decrease of protein prenylation levels, defective autophagy and increase of IL-1β secretion, followed by cell death. Since 25-hydroxycholesterol (25-HC), a metabolite of cholesterol, can suppress IL-1β production, thus reducing inflammation, we evaluated the effect of 25-HC in an in vitro model of mevalonate pathway alteration, obtained using Lovastatin. Human glioblastoma cell line (U87-MG) was chosen to mimic, at least in part, the central nervous system impairment observed in MKD; 25-HC effects were evaluated aimed at disclosing if this compound could be considered as novel potential drug for MKD. Our results showed that 25-HC is able to reduce inflammation but it is ineffective to restore autophagy flux and to decrease apoptosis levels, both caused by lower protein prenylation; so, in spite of its anti-inflammatory action it is not useful to rescue defective prenylation/autophagy impairment-driven apoptosis in Lovastatin impaired mevalonate pathway. We hypothesize the presence in the mevalonate pathway of alternative mechanisms acting between inflammation and apoptotic autophagy impairment.

Mammalian cells must maintain an intracellular reducing environment for survival (1). Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are generated as normal cellular metabolic byproducts (2), but an increase in ROS levels can induce oxidative stress that can lead to an inflammatory response (2). The thioredoxin system (thioredoxin/thioredoxin reductase/NADPH) is a crucial ubiquitous mechanism that protects against oxidative stress by its disulfide reductase function (3, 4, 5). The thioredoxin system is essential for mammals, as mice without thioredoxin-1 die shortly after implantation (6).

Thioredoxin-Interacting Protein (TXNIP) is a member of the arrestin domain–containing protein family (4, 7, 8). Members of this protein family, including TXNIP, play important roles in gluconeogenesis (9, 10, 11), adipogenesis (12), and fructose metabolism (13, 14). The absence of TXNIP can cause hyperlipidemia (15), hypoglycemia (11), decreased hepatic glucose production (HGP) (11), obesity (16), and increased beta cell survival (17). The TXNIP protein also participates in the regulation of peripheral glucose metabolism in humans (18). TXNIP is distinct from the other arrestin domain–containing proteins in its ability to bind to thioredoxin (4). TXNIP binds covalently to reduced thioredoxin and thus can inhibit thioredoxin disulfide reductase activity in vitro (19). TXNIP does not interact with oxidized thioredoxin or catalytic mutants of thioredoxin (4). The biochemistry of the TXNIP–thioredoxin bond is well characterized (4, 19, 20, 21). The key cysteine C247 of TXNIP is required for interaction with thioredoxin, as revealed by biochemistry and crystallography experiments (19, 20).

Transmembrane 7 Superfamily Member 2 (TM7SF2) is a transmembrane protein that resides in the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear membranes and has C14-sterol reductase activity to assist the conversion of lanosterol to cholesterol in mammalian cells (22). In addition to its role in cholesterol biosynthesis, the Tm7sf2 gene can regulate insulin signaling (23, 24) and inflammation (25). In mice, Tm7sf2 was recently identified to be a tissue-specific nuclear envelope transmembrane protein that directs liver-specific patterns of radial genome organization for gene positioning (24). In addition to being a liver gene expression regulator, human TM7SF2 has also been shown to interact with an intracellular redox sensor protein in vitro (26).

The mechanism of diet-related insulin resistance is incompletely resolved. Improving diet-induced hepatic insulin resistance is a primary target for the cure of type 2 diabetes. Akt phosphorylation and consequent suppression of gluconeogenesis are central to the liver insulin response, but how hepatocyte signaling networks are dysregulated during a high-fat diet (HFD) and oxidative stress remains unclear. Increased oxidative stress has been extensively studied in metabolic diseases, including insulin resistance (27). Since TXNIP is molecularly positioned to sense redox potential and regulate metabolism, we explored the role of the unique redox-sensitive cysteine of TXNIP in mammalian metabolism. Our results show that mice with genetic editing of this single cysteine in TXNIP have altered lipid species profiles, increased hepatic insulin sensitivity and signaling, and decreased liver inflammation in the setting of an HFD. We also show that expression of Tm7sf2 is elevated in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers, and Tm7sf2 can regulate the insulin signaling pathway in liver cells under ROS-stress conditions, providing insight into the underlying mechanism of insulin resistance in hepatocytes during oxidative stress. We provide data that a cholesterol biosynthesis transmembrane protein plays an unexpected role in providing a missing link between oxidative state and hepatic insulin signaling. Together, our findings define a fundamental intersection between redox biology and mammalian hepatic metabolism.

We first sought insight into the role of the TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction in different organisms. Gathering data through available protein databases for TXNIP, we observed that the “..HIISGTCASW..” amino acid sequence that is known to bind human thioredoxin based on human TXNIP–thioredoxin coexpression studies (20) and includes the key C247 residue is only present in mammals (Fig. 1A). Most fish also bear a cysteine residue at approximately position 250 in a similar “..HIISGMCDMW..” amino acid sequence; it is currently unknown whether the piscine TXNIP binds thioredoxin. To evaluate the role of the TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction on in vivo metabolism, we generated a TXNIP C247S (or C247S) mouse model using the CRISPR–Cas9 technique. For the conversion of the cysteine 247 residue to serine, we mutated the TGC sequence to ATG in exon 5 (Fig. 1B). Cysteine and serine differ only in the exchange of a sulfur atom with oxygen; therefore, the amino acid position retains similar size while losing its redox sensitivity (28). The mutation was confirmed by both a new SpeI restriction site generated by the ATG mutation and Sanger sequencing (Fig. S1, A and B). We backcrossed the knock-in alleles for five generations to breed out potential off-target modifications and confirmed Mendelian ratios of allele inheritance. We also performed targeted locus amplification (TLA) sequencing to ensure the accurate integration of the mutated sequences into the native TXNIP loci, with no evidence of incorrect or off-target integration events (Fig. S1C). The pups appeared healthy, with a normal phenotype. We followed the body weights of the mice from 6 to 12 weeks of age and found no difference between groups by 12 weeks of age (Fig. S1D).

We performed insulin tolerance tests (ITTs), glucose tolerance tests (GTTs), and pyruvate tolerance tests (PTTs) on 12-week-old chow-fed WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice. TXNIP KO mice were more insulin sensitive compared with WT mice as previously described (16), but we did not observe more insulin sensitivity in TXNIP C247S mice compared with WT mice (Fig. 1, C–E). We collected plasma samples from chow-fed WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice after a 4-h fast to assess plasma lipid profiles. A hexosylceramide (d18:1/20:0) was measured to be lower in plasma of the TXNIP C247S group compared with the WT and TXNIP KO groups (Fig. 2A). Lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) are essential plasma lipids that control oxidative stress, NLR family pyrin domain–containing 3 (NLRP3)-mediated inflammation, and inflammatory markers such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (29). Since there were alterations in the lipid metabolism of TXNIP C247S mice, we placed these mice on a 60% HFD for 8 weeks to study their metabolic phenotypes under high fat–induced ROS-stress conditions. Following an HFD, TXNIP C247S mice had improved insulin tolerance compared with WT mice but did not have improved glucose or pyruvate tolerance (Fig. 2, G–I). As in controls, TXNIP KO mice also had elevated insulin sensitivity compared with WT mice as expected (16) (Fig. 2G).

To delineate the organs responsible for improved insulin sensitivity, we performed a standardized hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp experiment with [3-3H]glucose infusion to assess whole-body glucose turnover and HGP and a bolus injection of [1–14C]2-deoxyglucose to measure insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in individual metabolic organs in 8-week HFD-fed mice. We and others have previously shown that TXNIP KO mice are more insulin sensitive compared with WT mice after an HFD (16, 34, 35). Both TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice showed increased insulin sensitivity compared with the WT mice, and TXNIP KO mice were more insulin sensitive than TXNIP C247S mice based on the glucose infusion rates during insulin clamps (Fig. 3A). Hepatic insulin action, measured as insulin-mediated suppression of HGP, was increased significantly in the TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice compared with WT controls after an HFD (Fig. 3C). This was due to a lower HGP during the insulin clamp, whereas basal HGP was not altered in these groups (15.9 mg/kg/m for WT, 20 mg/kg/m for TXNIP C247S, and 21.5 mg/kg/m for TXNIP KO groups), indicating the improved ability of insulin to inhibit gluconeogenesis in the livers of TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice (Fig. 3D). These data pointed to the protection of TXNIP C247S mice from HFD-induced hepatic and whole-body insulin resistance because of the single amino acid mutation in TXNIP protein compared with WT mice. Five-hour fasted insulin levels tended to be higher in HFD-fed WT mice than in TXNIP C247S (p = 0.06) and TXNIP KO mice. The lower insulin levels in TXNIP KO mice were consistent with improved insulin sensitivity in these mice (Fig. 3E). In contrast, insulin-stimulated glucose uptake rates in white adipose tissue (epididymal) were similar in TXNIP C247S mice compared with WT mice (Fig. 3F). Also, only the TXNIP KO group had elevated skeletal muscle glucose uptake rates compared with WT mice (Fig. 3G). These results suggest that increased insulin sensitivity in the TXNIP C247S group was primarily because of protection from diet-induced hepatic insulin resistance. Despite significant changes in insulin resistance in TXNIP C247S mice, we did not observe any differences in TXNIP protein levels (Fig. S1E). We also did not detect a difference in oxidative stress marker GSH and GSH/GSSG ratios between WT and TXNIP C247S mice livers under chow diet where insulin sensitivities are similar between WT and TXNIP C247S groups (Fig. 3H). However, we noted lower GSH and GSH/GSSG values in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers compared with HFD-fed WT mice livers along with improved insulin sensitivity (Fig. 3I). There was no difference between groups for thioredoxin activity (Fig. S2A) between the TXNIP C247S group and WT group livers. There was no correlation between body weight and hepatic insulin action levels of the mice included in the hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp studies (Fig. S2B). To confirm increased insulin signaling in the livers of TXNIP C247S mice, we performed Western blot analyses on insulin-stimulated tissues and detected increased Akt phosphorylation in the livers of the TXNIP C247S group compared with WT controls (Fig. 3J). These data suggest improved insulin signaling in the livers of HFD-fed TXNIP C247S mice. We did not observe a change in AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) or mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) phosphorylation in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers compared with HFD-fed WT livers (Fig. S2, C and D).

We measured liver free fatty acid levels in chow- and HFD-fed mice. We did not detect a difference between hepatic free fatty acid levels in the groups on a chow diet (Fig. S3A); however, the TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO groups tended to have decreased hepatic free fatty acid levels compared with WT controls on an HFD (Fig. S3B). We did not detect a difference in the liver triglyceride levels between groups (Fig. S3C). Plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate levels were elevated in TXNIP KO mice compared with WT and TXNIP C247S groups under chow diet and HFD (Fig. S3D). Liver hexosylceramide (d18:1, 20:0) and LPC levels of the WT and TXNIP C247S mice were similar following an HFD (Fig. S3, E–J).

One of the upregulated genes in TXNIP C247S mouse livers involved in cholesterol synthesis was particularly of interest. The Tm7sf2 gene codes for a protein that enables delta14-sterol reductase activity (22) and plays roles in several essential pathways. The TM7SF2 protein is a paralog of the Lamin-B receptor (LBR), which is also responsible for sterol reduction (24). This protein resides on nuclear and endoplasmic reticulum membranes (24). In the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway, the delta14-sterol reductase enzyme that the Tm7sf2 gene encodes can reduce C14-unsaturated sterols (36). The Tm7sf2 protein improves insulin sensitivity in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (23) and increases Akt phosphorylation in mouse livers (24), linking it to insulin signaling. Importantly, Tm7sf2 can control gene regulation in the liver, possibly through the protein’s ability to alter radial gene positioning within the nucleus (24). Moreover, Tm7sf2 controls the expression of several genes upstream and downstream in the cholesterol synthesis pathway (24). Because Tm7sf2 can affect both cholesterol biosynthesis and insulin sensitivity, we validated its upregulation by RT–quantitative PCR (qPCR) in a larger set of HFD-fed mouse livers (Fig. 5D).

Since Tm7sf2 was shown to alter Irs1/2 gene expression and positioning (24), we also tested for Irs1/2 mRNA expressions in mouse livers. Consistent with improved insulin signaling, we observed upregulated Irs2 mRNA expression in the HFD-fed TXNIP C247S mouse livers compared with WT and TXNIP KO mouse livers (Fig. 5E). On the other hand, we did not observe a significant difference in Irs1 mRNA expressions in the HFD-fed mouse livers (Fig. 5F). This finding agrees with prior studies that Irs2 plays a more dominant role in the liver and Irs1 in adipose tissue and skeletal muscles (37). Irs2 but not Irs1 is downregulated in the livers of subjects with metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (38) and obese subjects with type 2 diabetes (39). Notably, the upregulation of Tm7sf2 and Irs2 mRNA expressions in the livers of the TXNIP C247S mice was present only under HFD conditions but not under the control chow diet (Fig. 5, E–H). The increase in Tm7sf2 and Irs2 mRNA expressions in TXNIP C247S mouse livers also corresponded to a downregulation in Pck1 mRNA (Fig. 5I), which is the downstream target of the Irs2 pathway in the liver and suppresses gluconeogenesis (37, 39). We also detected higher Srebp2 mRNA expression in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers compared with WT and TXNIP KO mice, which is the upstream regulator of Tm7sf2 (Fig. S3P). These findings reveal Tm7sf2 as a potential mediator of improved hepatic insulin action in the HFD-fed TXNIP C247S mice.

After identifying Tm7sf2 as the potential mediator of insulin signaling in the livers of TXNIP C247S mice, specifically under HFD conditions, we sought to investigate whether Tm7sf2 controls insulin signaling in human liver cells under ROS stress. For this purpose, we used human HEPG2 cells that were transfected with either a Tm7sf2 plasmid or an empty vector control plasmid to overexpress the Tm7sf2 gene (Fig. S3R). We treated the oxidative stress group with 100 μM H2O2 to induce oxidative stress and stimulated the cells with human insulin. We chose to use H2O2 and not DTT since 100 μM H2O2 does not affect WT TXNIP–thioredoxin binding as DTT does (19). We observed the same outcomes as the mouse livers in the human liver cell line after ROS stress. Akt phosphorylation was increased only in redox-stress conditions (H2O2) by Tm7sf2 overexpression in HEPG2 cells compared with the empty vector group and not under the nonstressed condition (Fig. 6, A and B). Irs2 mRNA expression seemed to show a strong increasing expression trend (p = 0.054, ANOVA with post hoc multiple comparison testing) by Tm7sf2 overexpression with the oxidative stress in the H2O2-stimulated cells (Fig. 6C). Irs1 mRNA expression also appeared to be downregulated by Tm7sf2 overexpression with the oxidative stress in the H2O2-stimulated cells (Fig. 6D). The mRNA expressions of gluconeogenesis downstream target genes of Akt pathway in the liver, Pck1 and G6Pase, were also downregulated in the Tm7sf2-overexpressing cells but only under oxidative stress conditions (Fig. 6, E and F). Protein levels of PCK1–PEPCK were also lower in the Tm7sf2-overexpressing cells only under oxidative stress conditions (Fig. 6, G and H). Tm7sf2 can also control an anti-inflammatory response, and deletion of Tm7sf2 results in NF-κB activation and TNFα upregulation (25). Therefore, we also studied the NF-κB pathway in the HFD-fed mouse livers. We found that phosphorylation of both IkappaB kinase (IKK) and NF-κB p65 was decreased in TXNIP C247S mouse livers compared with WT controls and that downstream PKC activity was also decreased (Fig. S4, A–C). In addition, the Tnfa mRNA expression increase observed in HFD-fed WT mouse livers did not occur in TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice (Fig. S4D). We also observed a decrease in NLRP3 protein level in the livers of the TXNIP C247S group consuming the HFD, which did not occur in control groups (Fig. S4E).

Here, we also present clinical data of a family with some members carrying the heterozygous TXNIP C247S variant (Fig. 7A). The affected female patient was first evaluated in 2016 when she was 11 years old with a 2-year history of fever episodes accompanied by sore throat, abdominal pain, and headache. These symptoms largely disappeared over time. She presents normal body weight/body mass index value and normal plasma cholesterol and glucose levels. We obtained DNA from the patient and her parents for trio sequencing. The TXNIP C247S variant was inherited from her mother, who has a history of difficulty with weight loss and glucose intolerance. The mother presented abnormal weight, cholesterol, plasma glucose and blood pressure levels, which recovered following bariatric surgery. No other relative has been addressed regarding the C247S variant. The variant TXNIP (NM_006472.6):c.740G>C, p.(Cys247Ser), chr1:g.145994635C>G (hg38), is novel, with no previous documentation in population databases such as the 1000 Genomes Project, dbSNP, or the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD), version 4.1.0. Other variants of TXNIP C247 are observed in human databases. GnomAD, version 4.1.0 lists four other rare missense variants at the same codon: p.Cys247Trp (minor allele frequency [MAF]: 1.24e-6), p.Cys247Tyr (MAF: 6.20e-7), p.Cys247Gly (MAF: 1.24e-6), and p.Cys247Arg (MAF: 2.48e-6). These genomic data confirm that TXNIP C247 mutations are identified in human databases, and mutations of this cysteine appear to be well tolerated in the heterozygous state.Figure 7Heterozygous TXNIP C247S mutation is tolerated in humans.A, pedigree and health conditions of a family where some members carry a heterozygous TXNIP C247S variant. B, schematic presentation of altered signaling in TXNIP C247S livers (figures created using BioRender). C247S, Cysteine 247 for Serine; TXNIP, Thioredoxin-Interacting Protein.

Heterozygous TXNIP C247S mutation is tolerated in humans.A, pedigree and health conditions of a family where some members carry a heterozygous TXNIP C247S variant. B, schematic presentation of altered signaling in TXNIP C247S livers (figures created using BioRender). C247S, Cysteine 247 for Serine; TXNIP, Thioredoxin-Interacting Protein.

Here, we show that the TXNIP–thioredoxin covalent interaction is necessary for developing HFD-induced hepatic insulin resistance. Among the altered cholesterol biosynthesis genes upregulated with the removal of the key C247 cysteine that allows the TXNIP–thioredoxin bond, the Tm7sf2 gene may play a key role in improving insulin signaling in mice and human liver cells (Fig. 7B). Furthermore, a heterozygous form of the TXNIP C247S variant appears well tolerated in humans. This suggests a specific evolutionarily conserved mechanism where redox state interacts with insulin resistance through this one specific cysteine in the TXNIP protein, presenting a key role. An HFD is known to induce ROS stress in organs, including the liver (40, 41), pancreas (42), intestines, and brain (43). While we did not observe a significant difference in glucose metabolism of TXNIP C247S mice compared with WT mice under a chow diet, the improved insulin sensitivity phenotype was clearly apparent after an HFD.

The TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction is important for diverse processes in mammals, including glucose metabolism and insulin signaling, inflammation, and mitochondrial metabolism (44). During the hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic assays, we assessed the insulin-stimulated glucose metabolism in liver, skeletal muscle, and white adipose tissues of the mice to define the major organ affected by the loss of TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction. According to results of hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamps, the liver was identified to be the main site that the increase in insulin sensitivity was mainly observed. We did not detect and increase in insulin sensitivity other major metabolic organs such as white adipose and skeletal muscle tissues.

The regulation of TXNIP activity is crucial for redox balance. However, TXNIP also regulates redox-independent physiological effects that directly influence pathophysiological processes, such as inflammatory responses, disrupted glucose metabolism, cellular senescence, and tumor development (21). Our laboratory has previously shown in vitro that TXNIP regulation of glucose uptake is independent of its interaction with thioredoxin. Also ARRDC4, a close homolog of TXNIP with a similar arrestin domain but does not interact with thioredoxin, also has the ability to inhibit glucose uptake (45). Therefore, it is possible that TXNIP might also regulate arrestin domain–dependent and redox-independent effects on glucose metabolism, potentially explaining the distinctive phenotypes observed in TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice. Thioredoxin interaction is critical for redox-dependent functions of TXNIP (21). The structure of the thioredoxin–TXNIP complex shows that the interaction occurs through a redox-dependent disulfide bond switching mechanism. TXNIP C63 and C247 residues are also critical for TXNIP dimer formation (20). Even though the interaction is abolished with TXNIP C247S mutation, we did not observe a difference in thioredoxin activity levels in the liver after an HFD in TXNIP C247S or TXNIP KO groups, consistent with previous studies (11). This result suggests that TXNIP is not serving as a thioredoxin inhibitor in this setting; instead, TXNIP may be sensing the redox state and changing its molecular binding partners, as suggested by mass spectrometry experiments (46, 47). However, it is possible that the C247S mutation alters lipid and glucose metabolism by making more unbound thioredoxin available, even though we did not detect a difference in thioredoxin activity.

We found elevated Irs2 expression but not Irs1 expression in the HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers. This finding agreed with selective downregulation of IRS2 during insulin resistance in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver diseases (38). IRS2 plays a more critical role in insulin signaling in the liver than IRS1, which dominates in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue (37), particularly in the suppression of gluconeogenesis genes (38). Significant downregulation of hepatic IRS2 but not IRS1 expression in obese individuals with type 2 diabetes was also observed in comparison with nondiabetic obese patients (39). Our data agree with these studies, since Irs2 expression was increased and gluconeogenic signaling was decreased in TXNIP C247S livers.

The limited number of genes with expressions altered significantly with TXNIP C247S mutation suggests that this single amino acid mutation explicitly regulates the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway genes, including Tm7sf2, which also acts as a liver-specific gene positioner (24). The TM7SF2/NET47 protein is a member of a protein family that includes more than a hundred transmembrane proteins that reside on the nuclear envelope and that are constantly trafficked between the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear membranes (48). TM7SF2 is preferentially expressed in the liver (48) to control both the position and expression of liver metabolism–specific genes (24). Interestingly, in Tm7sf2-KO mice, which have insulin sensitivity, only a set of 26 genes changed position and expression (24), which agrees with our limited number of altered genes.

We found that Tm7sf2 mRNA expression was elevated in the livers of C247S mice specifically under an HFD. TM7SF2 itself can bind NADPH and act as an oxidoreductase (49). TM7SF2 is predicted to be a part of a receptor complex (Alliance of Genome Resources), and previous research has shown that it can interact with the redox sensor protein HSCARG/NmrA like redox sensor 1 (NMRAL1) that also binds NADP (26). TM7SF2’s elevation in livers and liver cell lines, specifically under ROS stress, and interaction with oxidative stress sensors, suggests that it could be serving as a part of a redox-sensing receptor complex that links intracellular redox state to insulin signaling.

Although our results suggested a role for Tm7sf2 in regulating insulin signaling during oxidative stress in liver cells, with a molecular response correlating with findings in the TXNIP C247S mice, in the light of the current data we cannot determine causality between the Tm7sf2 expression and the TXNIP C247S phenotype. To causally link the Tmsf72 gene to TXNIP C247S phenotype in mice further in vivo glucose metabolism experiments should be performed in double-transgenic Tm7sf2 KO/TXNIP C247S mice in future studies.

Even though cholesterol biosynthesis genes were upregulated, we did not observe a significant difference in plasma and liver cholesterol levels in TXNIP C247S mice. Liver cholesterol synthesis fuels the essential supply of animal cell plasma membranes and is very responsive to dietary cholesterol intake (∼100-fold), which in turn controls plasma cholesterol levels (50, 51). Therefore, it was unsurprising to find unaltered plasma cholesterol levels in these mice. Furthermore, a total KO of the Tm7sf2 gene in mice did not impair cholesterol biosynthesis (52) even though it controls both upstream and downstream cholesterol biosynthesis genes (52). The reason that Tm7sf2 KO mice did not have altered cholesterol levels was suggested to be due to LBR protein with redundant functions (22). Tm7sf2 and lamin-B receptor (lbr) genes emerged through a gene duplication event (53), and they share the same C14-sterol reductase activity (54). It was shown that Tm7sf2 expression levels showed an opposite trend compared with that of lbr in livers (54, 55). Expression of one could thus increase to compensate for the decrease of the other. This could contribute to the similar liver cholesterol levels in our mouse groups. Furthermore, in HFD-fed mouse livers, cholesterol synthesis genes were found to be downregulated, whereas plasma cholesterol levels were elevated (56), suggesting that expression of hepatic cholesterol synthesis genes does not reflect peripheral cholesterol profiles. Also in our model, the lipid changes observed in circulation did not seem to have a significant direct effect on insulin sensitivity.

The TXNIP C247S mutation was also found to significantly benefit visual acuity during retinitis pigmentosa in mice (57). The activation of the insulin pathway is beneficial to retinitis pigmentosa cone survival (58), so improving insulin signaling by TXNIP C247S mutation could contribute to this amelioration of sight. In addition, our TXNIP C247S mutation was global. Although we primarily observed glucose effects in the liver, an HFD would also alter cytokine and hormone profiles in adipose tissue. We cannot exclude interorgan crosstalk as a potential factor in these experiments.

The evolutionary basis for insulin resistance has been intensely debated for decades (59, 60, 61). One concept is evolutionary mismatch, where genetic changes that were initially advantageous in some manner, lead to insulin resistance in the modern setting of a calorie-dense diet (59, 62, 63). We speculate that mammals may have retained the TXNIP interaction with reduced thioredoxin through TXNIP C247, whereas amphibians, reptiles, and other animal classes lost this interaction. It is interesting that fish may have retained a different cysteine motif nearby; however, it is not known if the cysteine of TXNIP in fish allows covalent binding with thioredoxin. In settings of infection or injury, oxidative stress could promote hepatic insulin resistance to increase energy availability (62). Insulin resistance also progresses much faster during rapid growth periods such as puberty, possibly to enable energy redistribution (64, 65, 66). Thus, the TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction could potentially represent a mechanism for the redistribution of energy in times of stress, with possible detrimental cost of hepatic insulin resistance in the setting of a calorie-dense diet.

We generated a new TXNIP C247S mouse model using CRISPR–Cas9 technology. Our strategy was to swap the TGC codon in exon 5 of TXNIP that codes for the key cysteine to an AGT serine codon, and this change also creates an SpeI digestion site (Figs. 1B, S1A). Injections of the zygotes were carried out by the Genome Modification Facility at Harvard University. Zygotic pronuclei were microinjected with purified Cas9 mRNA (100 ng/μl), in vitro–transcribed synthetic guide RNAs (Synthego), and an asymmetrical ssDNA donor construct (IDT). Microinjected zygotes were implanted into C57BL/6J surrogate females. Genotypes were confirmed by restriction enzyme digestion and Sanger sequencing (Fig. S1, A and B), and 100% mutated mice were used as colony founders. Selected mice were bred with WT C57BL/6J mice, and pups were genotyped to confirm that the desired C247S mutation was incorporated into the germline. TLA sequencing was performed by Cergentis on cells from the frozen bone marrow of TXNIP C247S and WT controls that were processed according to Cergentis' TLA protocol (67) to check for off-target mutations. This analysis aimed to identify breakpoint sequences of the genomic modification(s) and assess the presence of structural variants surrounding the TXNIP locus. No other sequence and structural variants were detected in the TXNIP gene locus chr3:96,557,957-96,561,857 other than the desired mutation (Fig. S1C). Before experiments, mice were backcrossed in a C57BL/6J genetic background for several generations. WT siblings from the TXNIP C247S colony backcrosses were used to generate WT control mice. TXNIP KO mice were previously created by our laboratory (68). Male mice were used for metabolic studies involving insulin sensitivity because of increased variability in females because of hormonal changes (69). All mice were housed at a controlled temperature and a light–dark cycle with free access to a standard chow diet (Prolab IsoPro RMH 3000 5P75; LabDiet) or 60% HFD (D12492i; Research Diets) and water.

Mice were fasted for 16 h before GTTs and PTTs and 4 h before ITTs. Fasted mice were injected intraperitoneally with glucose (1 or 2 g/kg), pyruvate (1 or 2 g/kg), or insulin (0.75 or 1 IU/kg) according to their diet. Blood samples were collected via the tail vein, and glucose levels were measured using a handheld glucometer (Contour) at designated time points. Insulin stimulation was performed by injecting insulin (1 U/kg) i.p. and collecting liver tissues after 10 min.

HEPG2 human liver cell lines from American Type Culture Collection were cultured with a complete growth medium with Eagle’s minimum essential medium. Cells were transfected with EV or Tm7sf2 vector (NET47 pEGFP-N2 [593] was a gift from Eric Schirmer, Addgene plasmid #61986) using Lipofectamine 3000 reagent (Thermo Fisher). After 48 h, cells were starved in serum-free Eagle’s minimal essential medium for 4 h and were stimulated with 100 μM 30% H2O2 during the last 2 h. Later, cells were stimulated with 10 nm human insulin for 10 min and then collected, and protein and RNA samples were isolated.

Insulin levels were measured in 4-h fasted plasma using ELISA kits according to the manufacturer's protocol (Alpco; #NH80-INSMSU-E01). Liver thioredoxin activity was measured in liver lysates in a sample buffer using a modified protocol from Cayman Chemicals. Liver free fatty acids were measured in chow and 8-week HFD-fed mouse livers using a Free-fatty-acid Assay Kit (Abcam; #ab65341). PKC activity was measured by PKC Kinase Activity Assay Kit in liver lysates (Abcam; #ab139437). The kit measures the activity of all PKC isoforms. Liver triglycerides were measured in 8-week HFD-fed mouse livers using a Triglyceride assay kit (Abcam; #ab65336). Plasma and liver total and free cholesterol levels were measured using a Cholesterol quantification kit (Sigma–Aldrich; #MAK043). Plasma beta hydroxybutyrate levels were measured using ketone body kits (Abcam; #ab83390, #ab272541). Liver GSH/GSSG values were measured using GSH/GSSG Ratio Detection Kit II (Abcam; #ab205811).

Western blots were performed using Phospho-Akt (Ser473) (#9271), Akt (#9272), Beta-actin (#8457), Phospho-IKKa/b (#2697), IKKb (#8943), Phospho-NFkB p65 (#3033), NFkB p65 (#8242), Pck1 (#12940S), NLRP3 (#15101S), AMPKa (D5A2) (#5831) p-AMPKa (#2535), p-mTOR (#5536), and mTOR (#2972) antibodies (Cell Signaling). Protein bands were detected using an enhanced chemiluminescence substrate. Images were taken either using an automated processor (Bio-Rad) or with autoradiography films that were exposed in cassettes in a darkroom. Antibody validation was based on our previous publications, and preliminary experiments and expected molecular weights were observed. ImageJ (US National Institutes of Health [NIH], https://imagej.net/ij/, 1997–2018) software was used to quantify western blot images.

Lipidomic analysis of plasma samples was performed as described by Su et al. (70). Briefly, after the addition of an internal standard mix, lipids were extracted from plasma samples using an adjusted methyl tery-butyl ether–methanol extraction (71). Extracted lipids were concentrated and reconstituted in a mixture of dichloromethane:methanol (50:50) containing 10 mM ammonium acetate before shotgun lipidomic analysis. Samples were directly infused into the mass spectrometer using a Shimadzu HPLC (Nexera LC-30AD). Separation and targeted profiling of lipid species was performed by combining differential mobility spectrometry and a QTRAP system (QTRAP 5500; SCIEX) run in multiple reaction monitoring mode. Data analysis and absolute quantification of lipids were conducted using the Shotgun Lipidomics Assistant, a Python-based application that facilitates differential mobility spectrometry–based lipidomics workflow (70).

Mice that were fed 8 weeks of HFD were sacrificed, and liver tissues were collected. RNA was isolated using QIAGEN RNeasy Kits. RNA samples were processed by Azenta Biosciences for library preparation and Bulk RNASeq reads (Illumina). Bioinformatic analysis was performed using raw FASTQ as follows: The reads were trimmed for quality and adapters with Trimmomatic v0.39 (72) with the following parameters: LEADING:3 TRAILING:3 SLIDINGWINDOW:4:15 MINLEN:36. The standard Kallisto index was retrieved from Pachter Lab’s Github (https://github.com/pachterlab/kallisto-transcriptome-indices). Sequence-based bias correction was performed using Kallisto v0.50.1 (73) with 100 bootstraps. The transcript-level abundances from Kallisto were summarized and imported into R as a matrix of counts using tximport v1.0.3 (74). Differentially expressed genes were determined by estimating fold change and dispersion using DESeq2 (75). Pseudogenes and mitochondrial genes, as identified by Ensembl (76), were first removed from the dataset. Subsequently, the remaining data were filtered based on a p value threshold of 0.05, followed by a two-tailed t test with a significance level of 0.05. These significant genes were visualized using pheatmap, v1.0.12 (77) and ggplot2 v3.4.4 (78). Pathway analysis was performed using pathfindR (79) (v2.4.1) using the Kyoto Encylopedia of Genes and Genomes database (80). Reactome and WikiPathways enrichment analysis was performed using Enrichr, using The Reactome Pathways Knowledgebase 2024 and WikiPathways 2024 Mouse database, respectively. Bar charts of the results were plotted using Matplotlib and Seaborn using Enrichr Appyter.

For verification of RNA-Seq results, gene expressions were measured by RT–qPCR in a different cohort of mice. For RT–qPCR, RNA was extracted from homogenized liver samples and cells by the TRIzol (Life Sciences) method according to the manufacturer's protocol. The complementary DNA was synthesized from 2 μg of total RNA by use of the High-Capacity cDNA synthesis kit (Applied Biosystems), and reactions were performed using the Taqman gene expression assays (#Mm00840455, #Mm00443258, #Mm01277042, #Mm00514571, #Mm00501703, #Mm03038438, #Mm00440636, #Mm01233546, #Mm00839336, #Mm01278327, #Mm01337454, #Mm00477897, #Mm0490968, #Mm00436772, #Mm03012094, #Mm01306292, #Hs02802676, #Hs00159918, #Hs00427620, #Hs00178563, #Hs00275843, #Hs00162807, #Hs01098079; Thermo Fisher).

To generate the protein phylogeny tree in Figure 1, orthologs were pulled from Ortho DB v11 (81), National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database, and UniProt (82). The sequences were compared with NCBI COBALT (83), and iTOL and phyloT (84) software were used for tree generation.

Hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp experiments were conducted at the UMass Metabolic Disease Research Center using a primed and continuous infusion of human insulin (2.5 mU/kg/min), and glucose was infused at variable rates to maintain euglycemia (69). Briefly, whole-body glucose turnover was measured using a continuous infusion of [3-3H] glucose during the clamp, and HGP was determined by subtracting the glucose infusion rate from the whole-body glucose turnover. At the end of the clamps, mice were anesthetized and individual tissues were taken for biochemical analysis (69).

Data were expressed as means ± STD. The significance of the difference in mean values was determined using one-way and two-way ANOVA with Tukey and Bonferroni, Holm–Sidak post hoc tests, and Kruskal–Wallis test with Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli corrections and Student's t test where applicable. The statistical significance was set at a p value of <0.05.

All animal studies were performed in accordance with the NIH guidelines and approved by The Harvard Faculty of Arts and Sciences Standing Committee on the Use of Animals in Research (16-05-271/273). Patients were enrolled on NIH protocol 94-HG-0105 (NCT00001373). This study was approved by the “NIH Institutional Review Board” and complied with all relevant ethical regulations. Written and informed consent was obtained from all participants. Participants were not compensated for their participation. Human studies reported in the article abide by the Declaration of Helsinki principles.

The bulk RNA-Seq data are deposited into NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus profiles with accession number GSE275407.

This article contains supporting information (85, 86, 87, 88, 89, 90, 91, 92).

review_items.mechanism_name: De novo hepatic cholesterol biosynthesis via the mevalonate and post-squalene sterol pathway
review_items.mechanism_summary: Nearly all program genes encode sequential enzymes of the two-stage cholesterol biosynthesis pathway. The mevalonate arm (Hmgcs1 → Idi1 → Mvk → Pmvk → Mvd → Fdps → Fdft1) converts acetyl-CoA/mevalonate to farnesyl pyrophosphate and then squalene. The post-squalene arm (Lss → Cyp51 → Msmo1/Nsdhl/Hsd17b7 C4-demethylation complex → Tm7sf2 → Sc5d → Dhcr7) converts lanosterol to cholesterol. Erg28 is a non-catalytic scaffold protein that binds Nsdhl and Msmo1 to facilitate the C4-demethylation complex. Acss2 supplies acetyl-CoA from acetate as the carbon source. Scap and Insig1 directly regulate this entire biosynthetic program through SREBP2 activation in liver.

paper.title: Covalent binding of thioredoxin to TXNIP is required for diet-induced insulin resistance in the liver

review_items.selection_reason: Directly identifies Tm7sf2 as sterol reductase in cholesterol biosynthesis in HFD mouse liver

assessor_text.text:
Cholesterol, an essential compound of cell membranes, regulates permeability, fluidity, and membrane signaling capacity [1], is a precursor of steroid hormones and bile acids, and plays an important role in cell proliferation [2], [3]. Cholesterol originates from two sources – the dietary intake (30–50%) and de novo synthesis (50–70% in men) [4]. Its abnormal blood concentration leads to the increased risk of heart diseases and brain strokes. Thus, regulation on the cellular level and on the level of the entire organism is essential [5]. The lipid homeostasis is performed mainly by the liver, the major organ of lipid clearance [6] and synthesis. Almost 40% of the cholesterol is synthesized in the murine liver [7], and the pathway is well conserved in mammals. The loss of function of genes from cholesterol synthesis, metabolism or transport results in lethality or other serious conditions, where the severity of the phenotype depends on the position of gene in the pathway [8], [9], [10], [11]. Most murine studies focus on the complete knockout models that are unlikely to be found in humans, due to the lethal developmental phenotype, while mice heterozygous for the cholesterol-linked genes seldom present a distinct phenotype (Figure 1). However, the cholesterol homeostasis in humans exhibits examples where abnormalities manifest with the heterozygous variants, such as in the genes of cholesterol synthesis (HMGCR, DHCR7, DHCR24 and CYP51A1), where polymorphisms associate with preterm delivery or low birth weight [12], [13], [14].

Figure shows mouse characteristics in the cholesterol synthesis (A), bile acid synthesis pathways (B) and lipid transporters (C). In red are marked disease phenotypes, while in green are marked mild/no phenotype. *The heterozygous knock-out models often were not thoroughly investigated. Gene names and references to literature describing mouse models: Acat2 acetyl-coenzyme A acetyltransferase 2; Hmgcs1 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coa synthase 1; Hmgcr 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coa reductase [55]; Pmvk phosphomevalonate kinase; Mvd diphosphomevalonate decarboxylase; Mvk mevalonate kinase [56]; Idi1 isopentenyl-diphosphate delta isomerase 1; Ggps1 geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase 1; Fdps farnesyl diphosphate dynthase; Fdft1 farnesyl-diphosphate farnesyltransferase 1 [57]; Sqle squalene epoxidase; Lss lanosterol synthase; Cyp51 lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase [17], Tm7sf2 C-14 sterol reductase; Lbr lamin-B receptor; Sc4mol methylsterol monooxygenase 1*(WTSI); Nsdhl NAD(P) dependent steroid dehydrogenase-like [58], [59]; Hsd17b7 hydroxysteroid (17-beta) dehydrogenase 7 [60]; Sc5d lathosterol oxidase [61]; Dhcr7 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase [62]; Ebp emopamil binding protein (sterol isomerase) [63]; Dhcr24 24-dehydrocholesterol reductase [41], [64]; Cyp7a1 cholesterol 7-alpha-monooxygenase [65], [66]; Hsd3b7 3 beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 7 [67]; Cyp8b1 7-alpha-hydroxycholest-4-en-3-one 12-alpha-hydroxylase [68]; Cyp27a1 Sterol 26-hydroxylase [69]; Cyp7b1 25-hydroxycholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase [70]; Scrab1 scavenger receptor class b, member 1 [71]; Ldlr low density lipoprotein receptor [72]; Cd36 fatty acid translocase [73], [74]; Abcg5 ATP-binding cassette sub-family g member 5; Abcg8 ATP-binding cassette sub-family g member 8 [75].

The focus of our study is lanosterol 14α-demethylase CYP51, a cytochrome P450 from the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway. In humans, the CYP51A1 shows low nucleotide variability compared to other genes of the pathway and other related cytochrome P450 genes [15]. The mouse Cyp51 gene is 89% identical to the human counterpart [16]. The complete knockout of Cyp51 is embryonically lethal in mice [17]. In humans homozygous CYP51A1 dysfunctions have not been detected so far, as they probably spontaneously abort in early development. Cyp51 is likely not essential for normal spermatogenesis [18] even if the products of lanosterol demethylation might serve as signaling sterols [19]. In humans, CYP51A1 was hemizygously deleted in a family with cerebral cavernous malformations [20], and the gene was proposed as a candidate for the cause of pediatric cataracts [21]. The CYP51A1 heterozygous common variant (rs6465348) associates with the decreased birth weight in preterm babies and with the changed lipid profile in pregnant women [12]. Due to the crucial role of cholesterol synthesis for organisms’ integrity, the reported associations of CYP51A1 polymorphisms with brain function or early development likely represent only a portion of potential malformations caused by dysfunction of CYP51.

To assess the global role of decreased expression of Cyp51 by 50%, we investigated a large colony of Cyp51 heterozygous knockout (Cyp51+/−) mice of both sexes challenged with three diets differing in the fat and/or cholesterol content. The statistical modeling revealed novel associations between the Cyp51 genotype, the nutrition and the lipid homeostasis. Those factors, together with histopathology pinpointed to the liver as the most prominent disease target organ.

Heterozygous males Cyp51+/− (B6.129SV-Cyp51<tm1.1Bfro>) were obtained from the Department of Animal Science, Biotechnical Faculty, University of Ljubljana and mated with C57BL/6JOlaHsd females (Harlan, Italy). The experiments were performed at the Medical Experimental Center, Medical Faculty, University of Ljubljana. All the animals of over 95% of C57BL/6J background were housed 3–7 per cage (825 cm2 floor space) on Lignocel ¾ bedding material (Germany) in a 22–23°C room, 55±10% humidity and a 12 h light/dark cycle (illumination between 07.00 am −07.00 pm) with free access to food and acidified tap water (pH = 3). The experiment was approved by the Ethical Committee for laboratory animals of the Republic of Slovenia and Veterinary Administration of the Republic of Slovenia granted permit numbers 34401-31/2011/4 and 34401-29/2011/3. The experiment was conducted in accordance with the Directive 2010/63/EU on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes, as well as in accordance with National Institutes of Health guidelines for work with laboratory animals.

Litters were weaned at age of 3 weeks, genotyped as described [17] and randomly distributed to one of the diets for period of 16 weeks (8–15 mice/group; each group represents mice of specific gender and genotype on one of the diets):

LFnC (Low Fat no Cholesterol diet) (Item no. 1324 LFnC GmbH & Co. KG, Germany), a control diet with no cholesterol, supplying 2844 kcal/kg where 65% of the calories derives from carbohydrates, 24% from proteins and 11% from fat.

HFnC (High Fat no Cholesterol diet) – High Fat Clinton-Cybulsky rodent diet without cholesterol (D12106C, Research Diets INC, USA) supplying 4056 kcal/kg where 40.0% of the calories derives from carbohydrates, 20.0% from proteins and 39.9% from fat.

HFC (High Fat diet with Cholesterol) - High Fat Clinton-Cybulsky rodent diet with 1.25% cholesterol (D12108C, Research Diets INC, USA) supplying 4056 kcal/kg where 40.0% of the calories derives from carbohydrates, 20.0% from proteins and 39.9% from fat.

A total of 142 mice were sacrificed after a 5 h fast with cervical dislocation during the light period (11.30 am −2.30 pm) to limit diurnal variability. During the autopsy the mice were weighed; organs were removed, trimmed of adipose tissue, weighed and patho-morphologically examined. For the histology, left lateral lobe (lobus sinister lateralis) was fixed in 4% formalin and embedded in paraffin, sectioned (5 µm) and stained with hematoxylin and eosin. The rest of the liver was cut into small slices, snap frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C for further analyses. Immediately after cervical dislocation, the blood was taken from the right ventricle, collected into lithium-heparin coated tubes, and centrifuged for 15 minutes at 4°C at 3000×g; plasma was collected, snap frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C.

Liver sections of each mouse were scored individually for different parameters such as size, shape and polymorphism of the hepatocytes, nuclei and nucleoli, granulation of the cytoplasm, presence of inflammation, cholestasis, steatosis, apoptosis, mitosis, and potential abnormalities of bile ducts. Histological scoring was performed on hematoxylin and eosin stained sections in a blinded fashion by a pathologist, with a scoring system for steatosis as follows: no steatosis was assigned when less than 5% of hepatocytes contained lipid droplets, mild steatosis when 5–25% of hepatocytes contained lipid droplets, moderate when 25–50% of hepatocytes contained lipid droplets, severe steatosis when lipid droplets were present in 50–75% of hepatocytes, and very severe when lipid droplets were present in more than 75% of hepatocytes. Apoptoses and mitoses were counted on the whole liver section. Liver samples were taken in the same way for every mouse (vertical cut in the middle of the right lobe) to exclude variability due to technical preparation of the sample. Apoptotic cells were recognized by characteristic morphological features, such as chromatin condensation, cell shrinkage, and nuclear fragmentation [22]. Mitotic figures were identified according to the criteria proposed by van Diest et al [23]. Only cells with clear morphological features of metaphase, anaphase, and telophase were counted, avoiding apoptotic and hyperchromatic nuclei.

Plasma was analyzed by the Veterina Le Marechal d.o.o, Ljubljana by Architect Ci 8200 (Abbott Corporation, USA) using methods recommended by The International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC) and the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI), with original or recommended reagents: Total Cholesterol (TC) with Architect/Aeroseth 7D62 (Abbott), High Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (HDL) with Architect/Aeroseth 3K33-20 (Abbott), Triglycerides (TG) with Architect/Aeroseth 7D74 (Abbott) and Free Fatty Acids (FFA)/Non-Esterified Fatty Acids NEFA-HR (2) 436–91995 (Wako Chemicals GmbH). Non-HDL cholesterol (LDL) was calculated using the Friedewald equation [24]: LDL [mmol] = TC [mmol]-HDL [mmol]-(TG [mmol])/2.2).

Corticosterone was measured in plasma (5 animals/group, in duplicates) by a Corticosterone (Rat/Mouse) ELISA kit (EIA-5186, DRG Instruments GmbH) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Testosterone measurements in the males’ plasma were measured with the Testosterone (Rat/Mouse) ELISA kit (EIA-5179, DRG Instruments GmbH) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The average absorbance of samples was used for curve-fitting with Four Parameter Logistics using the ReaderFit software (https://www.readerfit.com/).

The total RNA was extracted from 30 mg of liver using the QuickGene RNA tissue kit SII (FujiFilm). RNA concentration was measured with NanoDrop ND-1000 and the quality (RNA Integrity Number) checked on RNA chips (Agilent). The total RNA (3 µg) in water was treated with amplification grade DNase I (Roche) by standard protocol and used immediately for the cDNA synthesis with the SuperScript III cDNA Synthesis Kit (Invitrogen). Real-time qPCR was performed with the LightCycler 480 using SYBR Green I Master according to instructions (Roche Applied Science). Primers were designed using the Primer3 software in a way that they would span over the intron and validated with melting and standard curve analyses (Table S1). The reaction was performed in a 5 µl volume using 3.75 ng of cDNA, 1.15 µl of water, 2.5 µl of SYBR Green I Master 2×, 0.3 µl of each 2.5 mM primers with the thermocycling program: 95°C for 10 min, then 95°C for 10 s, 60°C for 30 s, and 72°C for 5 s for 45 cycles plus a dissociation step (60–95°C). The relative expression was calculated as previously described [25]. Rplp0, Utp6c and Eif2a were selected for normalization as previously described [26].

The proteins were isolated from liver that was homogenized in lysis buffer (30 mg of tissue in 1 mL: 20 mM TRIS pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 10% glycerol, 5 mM EDTA, 1 mM PMSF and protease inhibitor cocktail Complete Roche) and incubated on an orbital shaker for 1 h at 4°C followed by 15 min centrifugation at 4°C and 12000 rpm. The protein concentration was measured with Pierce BCA Protein Assay kit (Thermo Scientific). The samples were separated by 12% SDS-PAGE and electro-transferred onto a PVDF membrane (Millipore, Eschborn, Germany). The membranes were blocked with 5% (w/v) nonfat dry milk in PBST containing 0.05% or 0.1% (v/v) Tween 20 for 1 h at room temperature. The membranes were then incubated with the appropriate primary antibodies (self-made rabbit polyclonal anti-CYP51 antibodies against the peptide QRLKDSWAERLDFNPDRY, 1∶2000; anti-HMGCR, 1∶1000, ABS229, Millipore, Billerica, MA, USA; anti-NSDHL, 1∶250, 15111-1-AP, Proteintech Group, Inc., Chicago, IL, USA; anti-TM7SF2, 1∶250, 12033-1-AP, Proteintech Group, Inc., Chicago, IL, USA; anti-GAPDH antibodies, 1∶5000, G9545, Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). Visualization was performed by goat anti-rabbit IgG peroxidase conjugate (1∶5000, A0545, Sigma Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) with 5% nonfat dry milk in PBST and chemiluminescence recorded.

The data was processed and analyzed using different R [27] and Bioconductor [28] packages. Linear regression modeling was employed using three predictor variables corresponding to genotype (Cyp51+/− and Cyp51+/+), sex (Female and Male) and diet (LFnC, HFnC and HFC) and 39 response variables corresponding to organ characteristics (7 variables), plasma parameters (7 variables), and hepatic gene expression (25 variables).

The package car [29] was used to estimate univariate normalizing transformation of the response variables by Box-Cox power transformation family on the predictors. The Box-Cox transformation of data was necessary, as gene expression results rarely present normal distribution and they were transformed with parameter λ close to 0, which is similar to logarithmic transformation. The transformed response variables were modeled using a linear modeling approach and empirical Bayes smoothing to the standard errors by the limma package [30]. A linear model was fitted using three predictor variables and their pairwise interactions.

Benjamini-Hochberg's method for controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) [31] was used to determine statistically significant response variables at significance level of α = 0.1. The significance level of α = 0.1 was chosen, due to small number of animals analyzed in each group. We wished to assess diet/gender/genotype effects on multiple and heterogeneous levels (i.e. globally). As this is (to our best knowledge) the first study of such kind, we have chosen a rather relaxed level of statistical significance (α = 0.1) in order not to miss more subtle, but important effects. The parameters that reached statistical difference close to α = 0.1 will be discussed as the trend and tendencies, but the main focus of the manuscript were differences significant at the level of α = 0.05. Differences between genotypes were assessed across all the mice as well as separately for each diet, sex and their combinations. HFnC and HFC diets were compared to the LFnC diet across all the mice as well as separately for each sex and genotype. Interaction between the diets and genotypes were estimated across all the mice, as well as separately for each sex. Figure S1 presents the hierarchical tree for assessing the Cyp51 genotype effect. Particular contrasts within the tree allow also studies of the diet – genotype interactions. The numbers of animals analyzed within each contrast (organs characteristics, plasma parameters, liver histology and hepatic gene expression) are shown in Table S2.

The Cyp51+/− animals on the standard laboratory diet (LFnC) develop normally based on standard visual inspection and as expected they reproduce normally [18]. The Cyp51+/− heterozygotes show a decreased expression of Cyp51 mRNA and protein compared to the Cyp51+/+ controls on each diet (Figure 2), indicating that Cyp51 is transcribed from both alleles with no compensatory mechanisms in Cyp51+/− mice. In wild types, the expression is higher on the two diets with no cholesterol (LFnC and HFnC compared to HFC), irrespective of the presence of excess dietary fats (HFnC) and is expectedly repressed on the high-fat, high-cholesterol (HFC) diet due to the cholesterol feedback regulation. A thorough investigation of the blood lipid panel, liver histology, and gene expression by linear regression modeling revealed other significant differences between Cyp51+/− mice and wild types.

Initially we evaluated the effect of Cyp51 genotype in sex-matched animals regardless of the feeding regime. This can simulate a random population where feeding is not controlled. The measured values of the body and organ weights, plasma lipids, steroid hormones and relative gene expression are shown in Table S3 with statistically significant features summarized in Table 1 and Figure 3. Cyp51+/− males had significantly increased plasma total cholesterol, HDL and LDL cholesterol (20–35% higher than controls) and present hepatomegaly (Table 1). On the other hand, Cyp51+/− females remained leaner than wild-type controls, with the plasma lipid profile similar to that of controls. The hepatic gene expression is summarized in Figure 3. As expected, the Cyp51+/− mice exhibited a decreased expression of Cyp51 and a trend of increased expression of majority of other cholesterogenic genes. The observed sexual differences (Nsdhl increased in females, Dhcr24 increased in males) require further investigation. On top of that, Cyp51+/− females had significantly increased expression of Abcg8 transporter, responsible for the cholesterol clearance to the bile, as well as the tendency of the increased expression of Cyp8b1 from alternative bile acid synthesis, and slightly decreased expression of fatty acid translocase Cd36. These changes in gene expression could aid in maintaining the healthier blood lipid profile of Cyp51+/− females compared to the males. The results from pooled population where mice ate either of the diets suggest that Cyp51 haploinsufficiency is more harmful for males than females.

While the global model suggested hepatomegaly only in Cyp51+/− males, the histopathology shows similar features in livers of both sexes, thus results are not separated according to the sex (Table 2 and Figure 4). On the standard laboratory diet (LFnC), livers of the Cyp51+/− mice show frequent apoptoses and mitoses compared to the wild-type mice. The apoptoses and mitoses were still present in Cyp51+/− mice on the high fat diets with or without cholesterol, yet less frequent than before, suggesting that dietary lipids partially rescued this phenotype. However, both high-fat diets in Cyp51+/− mice resulted in a moderate steatosis compared to mild steatosis of wild-types, indicating that whole body CYP51 and/or normal cholesterol synthesis may play a role in the hepatic accumulation of the fats.

In this part, we investigated how mice with one missing Cyp51 allele react to either a low-fat or high-fat diet, with or without cholesterol. On LFnC standard laboratory diet (low-fat, cholesterol-free), both Cyp51+/− and wild-types matched by sex had similar body and organ weights, as well as the plasma lipid levels (Table 3). In addition to the significantly reduced Cyp51 in heterozygotes of both sexes, Abcg5 transporter, which plays a role in the clearance of cholesterol to the bile, was increased in both sexes and Dhcr24 only in males (Figure S2 A).

On the diet with no cholesterol but with high fats (HFnC) there was similarly no changes in the body, organ weights and plasma lipids between Cyp51+/− and wild-type mice of both sexes. Sexual dimorphism was observed at the mRNA level of cholesterol synthesis genes. The majority of measured genes from this pathway were up-regulated in Cyp51+/− mice even if different genes show statistical significance in males and in females – the overexpression of Nsdhl and Dhcr7 in females and again Dhcr24 in males (Figure S2 B). A tendency of high NSDHL protein level was observed in both sexes. (Figure S3). From these data, we can deduce that the Cyp51+/− genotype is not immediately harmful for animals if at the high fat, cholesterol-free diet.

A dramatic influence on Cyp51+/− mice was observed on the high fat diet with 1.25% of cholesterol (HFC). The Cyp51+/− females remain significantly leaner compared to wild-types, with lower fat tissue/body weight ratio, and lower body weight, with increased plasma corticosterone (Table 3). The Cyp51+/− males have significantly enlarged livers compared to the wild-types. The expression of several genes from the cholesterol and bile acid synthesis is significantly increased in Cyp51+/− females compared to their controls. In females, the mRNA levels of Tms7Sf2 and Nsdhl were significantly higher in Cyp51+/− mice compared to controls (Figure S2 C), and TMS7SF2 also on the protein level, while the NSDHL protein dropped below the detection threshold (Figure S3 and Figure S4). This can be explained by the overall repression of cholesterol synthesis on the high-fat diet with cholesterol compared to other diets (Table S3). Interestingly, it appears that Cyp51+/− females repress cholesterol synthesis less effectively than males. From other pathways we noted a decreased expression of fatty acid translocase Cd36 in Cyp51+/− females, but not in males (Figure S2 C).

To further investigate the sexual dimorphism, we analyzed the Cyp51 genotype-sex interactions (Figure S5), which confirmed the significant differences in organ characteristics and in the expression of Cd36. The significant differences were found also in the expression of Cyp27a1 and Cyp7b1 from the alternative bile acid synthesis pathway, where Cyp51+/− females exhibited increased expression. Cyp27a1 is involved in bile acid synthesis pathway, but can also metabolize sterol intermediates from the cholesterol synthesis, including lanosterol [32]. The Cyp7b1 may also be involved in the development of atherosclerosis [33], oxysterol metabolism, and sex hormone synthesis. The elevated expression of this gene can play a role in the protective effect on cholesterol levels in Cyp51+/− females. On the other hand, the increase of Lpl expression was determined in the Cyp51+/− males, which should not be the case in the livers of adult animals [34] and can be indicative of an early phases of metabolic syndrome.

The analysis of diet-genotype interactions confirmed observed sexual dimorphisms, resulting in different patterns of gene expression in males and females. The cholesterogenic genes Nsdhl, Sqle, Cyp51 and Sc4mol increase in Cyp51+/− females when fed with HFnC diet compared to LFnC diet and decrease with cholesterol supplementation (HFC), whereas they are decreased in wild-type females when fed with either of the high-fat diets. On the protein level, we confirmed the decrease in NSDHL expression in Cyp51+/− females on HFC diet, and the decrease in its expression in wild-type females on both high-fat diets. The expression of Nsdhl, Sqle, and Tm7sf2 was still increased in lean Cyp51+/− females fed HFC compared to their wild-type counterparts, suggesting that the feedback regulation of their expression might be less efficient. The high-fat feeding triggered differential expression of Abcg5 transporter in Cyp51+/− males compared to the wild types, whereas in females more diet-genotype interactions were observed. The analysis of interactions did not discover differences in expression of nuclear receptors, leaving the mechanism of the observed phenotype unclear.

We questioned how the dietary fats affect the Cyp51+/− genotype is affected, in the absence of cholesterol (HFnC vs LFnC) or in the presence of cholesterol (HFC vs HFnC), which is the usual case in high-fat nutrition. The major impact was observed for the cholesterol and lipid homeostasis genes, which is shown in the expression plots (Figure 5).

Plots showing the change in expression levels in males and females, both Cyp51+/− (red) and Cyp51+/+ (blue). Grey color indicates a linear smooth of 0.95 confidence intervals. The significant interactions between factors (Cyp51 genotype and diet) that can be understood as the differences between slopes of lines are indicated by their p values.

The LFnC and HFnC diets were without significant amounts of cholesterol (<0.01%), so there is a need for the increased cholesterol synthesis. However, females and males adapt to this condition differently. Only females with the Cyp51+/−genotype increase the expression of genes from cholesterol synthesis on HFnC diet, while the adaptation is already present in wild-type males (Figure 5, Table S4). The difference is observed also at the level of Abcg5 (from direct clearance of cholesterol), where only the wild-type males, but not females increase the expression on high fat load (comparing LFnC and HFnC) (Figure 5, Table S4).

The cholesterol feedback regulation does not differ majorly between the Cyp51+/− and wild-type mice in the presence of dietary cholesterol, which is shown in an interaction study between Cyp51+/− vs Cyp51+/+ genotypes and high-fat diets with and without cholesterol (HFnC vs HFC). Results indicate that irrespective of the Cyp51 genotype, mice reacted similarly to cholesterol supplementation in the high-fat milieu (Table S4). Differences in the expression of Ldlr in females and Lpl in males were significant, but remained in the same direction in both genotypes (Figure S6, Table S4).

The genotype-phenotype correlation is a complex feature, where genes interacting with the environment can lead to less predictable phenotypes even in single-gene knockout models. To assess the global role of the decreased expression of Cyp51 from cholesterol synthesis, we investigated mice with one functional Cyp51 allele since the inactivation of both alleles led to the embryonically lethal phenotype [17]. We applied a controlled environment which mimics the human eating habits - mice of both sexes were on diets for 16 weeks and not only 1 to 8 weeks as used in many rodent studies [35], [36], including these from the Mouse Phenome Database (http://phenome.jax.org). A large data-set from the Cyp51+/− mice and corresponding controls was collected and analyzed by linear regression modeling taking into account the sexual dimorphism, which is characteristic for cholesterol homeostasis in rodents and humans [36], [37], [38].

It appears on first glance, the Cyp51 heterozygous knockout has a negligible effect, because mice seem to develop normally. A deeper analysis revealed significant changes in the phenotype on the organ and metabolic level. Overall, the Cyp51+/− males seem to be more affected than Cyp51+/− females, presenting hepatomegaly and an increased plasma lipid profile. The liver histology showed apoptotic and mitotic events in the Cyp51+/− mice of both sexes and on all diets (less severe with the high-fat), which was not observed in the wild-type mice and should not be found in livers of healthy animals. The hepatic apoptoses and mitoses are indication of pathological events in cells (such as toxicity, increased oxidative stress, increased accumulation of intermediates, inflammation, etc.), and they are biomarkers for severity of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) [39]. The Cyp51+/− females were leaner than wild-type littermates and did not show significant changes in the blood lipid profile compared to wild-types. They also did not show hepatomegaly, but displayed hepatic apoptoses, mitoses and increased lipid infiltration on high-fat diets, which may relate to a group of difficult to diagnose cases of “lean NAFLD” [40]. The extrapolation of metabolic data obtained from murine models directly to humans is not always straightforward. Additionally, the mRNA levels do not necessarily reflect the protein levels and enzymes activity. In our study we found a good correlation between mRNA and protein levels for CYP51 and NSDHL (and partially also for TM7SF2). This is true also for HMGCR where the expression did not differ significantly between the genotypes at the mRNA or protein levels (Figure S7). The liver is a major organ of cholesterol synthesis in mice, but in primates the synthesis mainly occurs in extra hepatic tissues. However, murine models proved to be a great tool investigating inborn errors of cholesterol and bile acid synthesis and phenotypes relate well to human individuals [9], [10]. It is thus plausible to speculate that human individuals of both sexes with functional polymorphisms in the CYP51A1 are at increased risk to develop liver pathologies.

Our results indicate that the diminished expression of Cyp51 from cholesterol synthesis was more harmful for males than for females. The male predominance was observed also for Dhcr24 as another cholesterol synthesis gene, where the viable Dhcr24−/− knockout males showed a more severe phenotype than females [41]. However, in our case, the female Cyp51+/− phenotype resembles the ‘lean NAFLD’ with increased corticosterone on the high-fat diet, which might represent another risk factor for rapid development of fatty liver disease. Additionally, the expression of genes from cholesterol synthesis in Cyp51+/− females appears to be more sensitive to the high-fat diet challenge. It appears that females (even Cyp51 wild-types) are sensing lack of cholesterol better than males (especially on the high fat diet) increasing the expression of cholesterol synthesis genes more efficiently than males, which improves the flux through the cholesterol synthesis pathway towards cholesterol [36].

The expression of cholesterogenic genes was shown to be sex-biased; however, data reported in literature are inconsistent [36], [42], [43]. We identified higher expression of several genes in females including Srebp2, Hmgcr, Lss and Ebp from cholesterol synthesis (Table S5), which is in line with Gatti et al [43] and relates well with Lorbek et al [36]. However, in our study we investigated sexual dimorphism in context of Cyp51 genotype and we uncovered novel differences at the level of expression of cholesterogenic genes. Knockout of one Cyp51 allele led to a reduced expression of the CYP51 protein in both sexes. The Cyp51 haploinsufficiency triggered the increased expression of Dhcr24 in males and Nsdhl in females. DHCR24 metabolizes different precursor sterols, including lanosterol which is the major substrate of CYP51 [44]. NSDHL accumulates on the lipid droplets where it is involved in storage of neutral lipids, such as triacylglycerol and cholesterol esters [45] and possibly contributes to the cholesterol clearance in Cyp51+/− females. The Nsdhl gene is located on the X chromosome and possibly due to a presence of a single copy cannot be overexpressed in males, but it seems to play an important role in the cholesterol homeostasis of Cyp51+/− females. The leaner Cyp51+/− females showed the increased expression of Cyp8b1 from alternative pathway of bile acid synthesis and Abcg8 from transport of cholesterol to bile suggesting increased cholesterol clearance. The decreased adipose tissue correlates with a healthier blood lipid profile in Cyp51+/− females and decreased expression of Cd36 accounting for the protective effect from cardiovascular diseases [46], [47] in Cyp51+/females, but not in males. The mechanism of observed sex differences cannot be explained by our current experimental design, but one possible explanation for sex differences could be in the interaction of lowered Cyp51 expression with female sex hormones [48], [49]. The sex hormone hypothesis is supported by the study of Romero-Aleshire et al [50] demonstrating that in the mouse menopause model, even without a high-fat diet treatment, progression into menopause caused a significant increase in the cholesterol levels indicating that estrogens might indeed play a role.

The global model focusing on differences observed only due to Cyp51 genotype show that Cyp51+/− males had significantly increased total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol compared to Cyp51+/+ mice, while Cyp51+/− females managed to maintain blood lipids on similar level as wild-types, possibly due to the increased clearance via Abcg5/8 transporters or modified lipids storage. Apparently, the diminished expression of Cyp51 was still sufficient for cholesterol synthesis, even in the absence of cholesterol in the diet, but resulted in increased mRNA of other cholesterogenic genes and that further led to dysregulation of lipid homeostasis. Heterozygous mice showed increased plasma cholesterol concentration, increased hepatic lipid storage and signs of metabolic stress (indicated by hepatic apoptotic and mitotic events in both sexes and increased corticosterone in females). The mRNA levels of nuclear receptors could not explain this phenotype and the mechanism of dysregulation of lipid homeostasis is yet to be discovered. The decrease in Cd36 and increase in gene expression from the bile acid synthetic pathway on HFC diet likely contributed to better management of the healthy blood lipid profile in Cyp51+/− females, but significantly increased corticosterone might represent an independent fatty liver risk factor [51]. Corticosterone is a stress hormone that, when elevated, can lead to changes in metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins, and lipid homeostasis, resulting also in the leaner phenotype in mice fed with high-fat diet [52]. The increased corticosterone does not always affect cholesterol levels in rodents [53], which was also the case in Cyp51+/− females. Because Cyp51+/− females were housed in the same manner as wild-types at all diet regimes, the increased corticosterone in Cyp51+/− HFC group suggests metabolic stress that could be a consequence of the loss of one Cyp51 allele.

The heterozygous mutations leading to the decreased protein levels or enzyme activity often result in mild phenotypes that can be easily overlooked. The cumulative effects of single mutations, which may cause very mild phenotypes independently, together with the environmental factors, carry important information about causes of complex diseases. It seems that much of the genetic control of common diseases is due to rare variants with a strong impact on disease risk in individual patients [54]. Our work shows that even heterozygous loss of function of one Cyp51 allele from the cholesterol synthesis leads to significant phenotype differences in male and female mice, where Cyp51+/− males are more affected by harmful cholesterol lipid profile and hepatomegaly, but also Cyp51+/− females reveal risk factors of the fatty liver disease. It is thus plausible to assume that the etiology of liver diseases differs between males and females, where cholesterol synthesis represents a crucial point of sexual dimorphism.
